summary: Assigns one of the reserved label values from RFC 3032 as the OAM Alert Label, used to identify user-plane MPLS operation and maintenance packets. This lets routers tell management test packets from ordinary traffic.

eli5.summary: Special health-check packets need a way to say I am a check, not normal mail. This note picks the special sticker that marks them.

subtitle: Reserves MPLS label value 14 so that operation and maintenance packets can be told apart from user traffic.

tldr.problem: Network operators need MPLS packets that carry fault detection and performance checks to be recognizable as such, rather than being mistaken for ordinary user data.
tldr.mechanism: One of the reserved label values from RFC 3032, the value 14, is assigned as the OAM Alert Label that marks user-plane MPLS OAM packets.
tldr.outcome: IANA reserved label 14 for this purpose, and the note explains how the ITU-T Y.1711 OAM functions behave when penultimate hop popping is in use.

today: RFC 3429 is an Informational RFC and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It records the IANA reservation of label 14 as the OAM Alert Label.

sections.title: What the Note Assigns
sections.content: RFC 3429 assigns one of the reserved label values defined in RFC 3032 (MPLS label stack encoding) to the OAM Alert Label. User-plane MPLS OAM functions use this label to identify MPLS OAM packets, as described in ITU-T Recommendation Y.1711.
sections.eli5: Out of a box of reserved stickers, one is picked to mean this packet is a health check.

sections.title: OAM Functions and Packet Identification
sections.content:
MPLS OAM (Operation and Maintenance) gives operators tools to run their networks, at the MPLS layer and independent of OAM at lower layers such as SONET/SDH. The listed objectives are defect and failure detection, reporting defect information to other management entities, defect localization, and performance monitoring (packet loss, transfer delay, bit errors and so on).

The user-plane mechanisms in Y.1711 use the OAM Alert Label to tell OAM packets from normal user packets. The value 14 is used for this. The ITU-T Study Group 13 work behind it includes Recommendations Y.1710 and Y.1711, with Y.1720 on protection switching still a draft under last call as of November 2002.
sections.eli5: Operators need to know if a road is broken, where, and how bumpy it is. Packets with the number 14 sticker carry those checks.

sections.title: Behavior with Penultimate Hop Popping
sections.content:
The note answers concerns raised at IETF meetings about penultimate hop popping (PHP), where the second-to-last router removes the top label. Y.1711 says its OAM functions apply to both non-PHP and PHP cases unless otherwise stated.

There are two PHP cases. In Case 1 the last node is an MPLS router that cannot do two lookups at line rate, so it asks for PHP with reserved label 3 (implicit null). In Case 2 the last node has no MPLS label lookup ability at all and also asks for PHP with label 3. Currently Y.1711 can only be applied to Case 1; Case 2 and carrier supporting carrier scenarios need further study.

In Case 1, the penultimate router pops the top label and forwards the OAM packet with the OAM label and payload intact. If the last router supports MPLS OAM, it knows an OAM packet has arrived because the OAM label is now on top, and it identifies the ingress router from the TTSI (Trail Termination Source Identifier). If it does not support MPLS OAM, the packet is discarded as per section 3.18 of RFC 3031.
sections.eli5: The second-to-last helper peels off one sticker, but leaves the number 14 sticker on. The last stop sees it and knows it is a check. If it does not know about checks, it throws the packet away.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has reserved MPLS label value 14 as the OAM Alert Label. The note raises no security issues beyond those already present in the MPLS architecture or in the network layer protocol carried inside the encapsulation.

It adds that OAM could improve security: the Connectivity Verification (CV) function in Y.1711 can detect mis-connections, and so can prevent one customer's traffic from being exposed to other customers.
sections.eli5: Number 14 is now officially saved for this job. The checks can even help spot packets sent to the wrong place.

references.text: Rosen, E., et al., "MPLS label stack encoding", RFC 3032, January 2001.
Rosen, E., Viswanathan, A. and R. Callon, "Multiprotocol Label Switching Architecture", RFC 3031, January 2001.
